title: The Internal Passive (Al-Fiʿl al-Majhūl)
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 18; Ryding Ch. 38)
objectives: Form the internal passive in the past (فُعِلَ) and imperfect (يُفْعَلُ).
Promote the direct object of an active clause to deputy agent (nāʾib al-fāʿil) in the nominative case.
Distinguish active and passive verbs by their internal vowel melody.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 12: In an active verbal sentence, what case does the direct object (mafʿūl bihi) take?

sections.heading: Internal Vowel Melodies for the Passive
sections.body: Arabic forms the passive voice (al-mabnī li-l-majhūl) internally by changing the vowel melody—without needing an auxiliary verb like 'was'. When a verb is made passive, the original agent (fāʿil) is omitted and the direct object becomes the deputy agent (nāʾib al-fāʿil).

sections.label: Passive Vowel Melody & Nāʾib al-Fāʿil
sections.summary: Past passive: ḍammah on the first vowel and kasrah before the final radical (فُعِلَ). Imperfect passive: ḍammah on the prefix and fatḥah before the final radical (يُفْعَلُ). The deputy agent (nāʾib al-fāʿil) takes the NOMINATIVE case (rafʿ).

sections.heading: Active vs. Passive Voice
rows: فَتَحَ الرَّجُلُ البَابَ ('The man opened the door')

sections.irab: كُتِبَتِ: فِعْلٌ مَاضٍ مَبْنِيٌّ لِلْمَجْهُولِ | الرِّسَالَةُ: نَائِبُ فَاعِلٍ مَرْفُوعٌ بِالضَّمَّةِ
sections.notes: Because الرِّسَالَةُ (nāʾib al-fāʿil) is feminine, the passive verb takes the feminine ending ـَتْ.

sections.heading: Classical Arabic Omits the Agent
sections.body: In pure Classical Arabic, the passive is used specifically when the agent is unknown or unmentioned; avoid translating English 'by X' literally with مِنْ قِبَلِ in classical style.
